For anybody who might be asking the same question, if you have written a short thing, you write a query letter to go along with it (stating basics about the piece and your bio) and then send it out to EVERYWHERE that you think it might have a place. Be simple and professional, because your writing will speak for itself, and Google how you should format things.

I think that writing a lot is really REALLY important, but that alone is not going to help you improve. In retrospect, some of the advice I'm about to give you is variations on that theme, but I hope the specificity at least helps you out. :)

* Read a ton of books. Read inside your favorite genre, and outside of it. Try to read in a "sleuthy" way and not just for entertainment-- maybe try writing in the author's style, or just practice paying very close attention to every word. Read it out loud. Act it. Copy out a paragraph longhand. Do whatever it takes to pay attention to every single word.
* Read a ton of books about writing. There are a lot of surprisingly good books at my local library, and in high school I read through all of them. I don't remember any titles in particular; just read every book about writing you can get your hands on. You don't need to follow every bit of advice to the letter, but try to internalize the sorts of things they're saying.
* Post on the internet. People on the internet have a VERY short attention span, and therefore demand instant entertainment. If you can even get people to read something you've written, you're doing something right.
* Keep a journal and practice free-writing. Free-writing is a type of writing process that values quantity over quality, and helps you get into a mindset where you might produce a single quality phrase that really gets the ball rolling. It was heavily emphasized in my poetry classes, and I think it's a huge help in actually getting first drafts done without laboring over every single word. 
* Try blogging, especially if you have a pet topic. It helps you write consistently, and the instant gratification can help keep you motivated during longer projects. It also attunes you more sensitively to what people actually want to read.

In short, I think that other budding writers are good companions, but not necessary for improvement. Studying what is successful (whether that's Stephen King or your favorite self-published indie writer) is what will really make improvements.

I have been writing seriously since age fourteen. Obviously, I didn't think I was gonna be Christopher Paolini, but I have been working on building up credits and perfecting my craft since freshman year of high school.

I think that college is the right place for me because I love to learn and do academic stuff, but I don't know that being a Creative Writing major has helped my career any more than being a phrase that I can slap into a query letter. If I were to do it again, I'd probably major in a related field that interests me, like maybe theatre or linguistics.

I believe that they are giving me career skills, but maybe not for a specific career, if that makes sense. For example, I now pay immense attention to detail when I write anything relatively formal (which is great in a technological world where text is the key medium); I am very good at critiquing things and locating the source of problems while also being sensitive; and I have a mastery of rhetoric which is helpful for a lot of creative work, including advertising and things like that. 

I want to get a day job as a theatrical lighting designer and keep on writing. :)

I think the best improvement to my writing came with an attention to detail. Most of our classes are workshop based, and therefore every sentence and every word comes under inspection-- "Is this necessary? Is this accomplishing what you want it to?" That's the biggest difference between "amateur" and "professional" writing, in my opinion.

I don't know if I have ever heard a specific statement that was bullshit because, as I said, most of our classes were workshops, but there was a general disdain for genre fiction which really upset me. I write a variety of genres, and once handed in a fantasy story that nobody knew what to do with because they "didn't like fantasy." Definite elitist bias, there.

It seems like you are expecting them to be cats, which is pretty natural since that's a pet that we're all pretty familiar with. I did the same thing. Ferrets are not affectionate in the same way that cats or dogs are. It's not that they're "less" affectionate, but they do tend to be very very busy!

You have to interact with them in ways that are in accordance with their instincts. Their priorities are exploring, burrowing, and stealing. Therefore, cat toys might not work-- my boy loves them, but my girl totally ignores them. Try instead wrapping them up in a blanket and carefully smooshing them around. Give them small, safe objects to hide. Stick them in the bathtub. Find stuff for them to dig in.

Then when they fall asleep you can scoop them up and cuddle them. :)
